title: More Comfortable Living, Wider Consumption Gaps? The Impact of China's "15-Minute Convenient Living Circle" Pilot Policy on Urban Consumption
affiliations: Tsinghua University, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law, Hunan Agricultural University and Zhongnan University of Economics and Law

detail.title: More Comfortable Living, Wider Consumption Gaps? The Impact of China's "15-Minute Convenient Living Circle" Pilot Policy on Urban Consumption
detail.abstract: This paper studies how a community-level service intervention reshapes urban consumption patterns. We exploit China's "15-minute Convenient Living Circle" (CLC) pilot policy as a quasi-natural experiment and combine it with high-frequency transaction data from 2018 to 2022 to estimate the causal effects of this policy on consumption behavior. We find that the CLC policy significantly increases aggregate consumption, while simultaneously shifting consumption toward more advantaged locations and thereby widening spatial inequality both within and across cities. The effects are stronger in larger and less-aging cities and are concentrated in service-oriented sectors. Mechanism analyses suggest that the policy operates in part through changes in transportation accessibility, local service density, and population mobility. Our findings highlight the role of place-based service interventions in shaping urban consumption patterns and reveal a trade-off between consumption growth and spatial inequality.

title: The Energy–Logistics–Cost Nexus: Assessing LCOE Volatility, Decarbonization Barriers, and SDG 7 Alignment
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Energy–Logistics–Cost Nexus: Assessing LCOE Volatility, Decarbonization Barriers, and SDG 7 Alignment
detail.abstract: As the global energy transition matures, analytical focus has shifted from isolated engineering performance toward integrated system-level economic efficiency. While the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) remains the universal metric for evaluating project viability, traditional models are largely static, failing to incorporate the profound financial impacts of supply chain performance, logistical volatility, and institutional constraints. This study addresses these "integration gaps" by examining the relationship between logistical system conditions, operational disruptions, and sustainability outcomes.Adopting a critical realist perspective and a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the research utilizes semi-structured interviews with industry experts to identify sources of operational friction, followed by Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and the development of an Integrated LCOE (I-LCOE) model. Central to the study is the Dynamic Logistics–Sustainability Integration Model, which conceptualizes renewable energy systems as interconnected layers where logistical agility directly influences financial risk.The findings establish logistics as a primary structural cost driver embedded across all project lifecycle phases. The research identifies "logistical velocity" as a critical determinant of the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), as supply chain friction serves as an aggressive risk multiplier that inflates investor risk premiums. Furthermore, physical upscaling of components introduces non-linear logistical constraints that traditional models fail to capture. The study proposes an integrated digital knowledge management platform to resolve information asymmetry. By internalizing traditionally externalized variables such as geopolitical disruptions at maritime chokepoints this research provides a transformative framework for achieving SDG 7 and optimizing the systemic costs of global decarbonization.

title: Coordinating hydrogen valley design with global energy systems and local constraints and opportunities - Part 1: Methodology
affiliations: Mines Paris - PSL, , affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Mines Paris - PSL

detail.title: Coordinating hydrogen valley design with global energy systems and local constraints and opportunities - Part 1: Methodology
detail.abstract: To achieve the energy transition, low-carbon hydrogen is considered as a key lever. Its deployment is expected to revolve around specific industrial hubs, commonly referred to as ``hydrogen valleys". These territories generally combine existing uses of fossil-based hydrogen with significant potential for future demand. However, their development raises several major challenges: resource availability, land use management, and the need for coordination with national or continental energy strategies. Moreover, local opportunities for synergies and infrastructure optimization can influence the equilibrium of the broader energy system, notably by shifting territorial attractiveness, hence, hydrogen demand, and investment needs. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a hybrid methodological framework combining two complementary modeling approaches. The first, based on MIRET-EU, a TIMES model of the European energy system, assesses the competitiveness of hydrogen relative to other energy carriers and identifies opportunities for local production within a global transition context. The second, based on PHOENIX, a MILP model for industrial zone optimization, designs local infrastructure by integrating territorial constraints such as resource availability, land use management, and synergy opportunities. The iterative loop between the two models is the strength of the methodological framework: European energy transition scenarios generated by MIRET-EU serve as inputs for PHOENIX, which then optimizes the local hydrogen value chain. Local results are subsequently fed back into MIRET-EU to adjust the system equilibrium. Through successive iterations, the approach converges toward a solution that is coherent with both macro-energy planning and territorial feasibility. This paper is the first of a series of two articles and focuses on the methodological framework. The second paper will demonstrate its relevance through a real case study.

title: AI-assisted reliability-constrained design and real-time optimization of circular waste-to-methanol systems under feedstock uncertainty
affiliations: Sungkyunkwan University, Sejong University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Sungkyunkwan University

detail.title: AI-assisted reliability-constrained design and real-time optimization of circular waste-to-methanol systems under feedstock uncertainty
detail.abstract: Circular production systems from waste-derived feedstocks are essential for advancing sustainable and resource-efficient operations. However, their deployment is challenged by inherent feedstock variability, which can adversely affect process stability, efficiency, and safe operation. This study proposes a reliability-constrained framework for the design and real-time optimization of a methanol production process from biogas. First, a process model of the integrated reforming and methanol synthesis system was developed to generate performance data. A residual neural network surrogate was then constructed to capture process behavior with low computational cost, achieving high predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.94). Multi-objective optimization using NSGA-II was applied to identify optimal operating strategies considering unit production cost (UPC), net carbon emissions (NCE), exergy efficiency (EXF), and methanol production of three configurations (P1–P3). The results show that the optimal methanol production rate, UPC, NCE, and EXF reached 346 kg/h, 0.63 USD/kg, −0.86 kg CO2/kg, and 50%, respectively, under different objective functions. In the real-time optimization of 30 days operation (a target reliability of 98%), P2 achieves superior robustness, maintaining stable production and reducing cumulative CO2 emissions by 8,300 kg, while P1 exhibits instability and frequent reliability violations. Overall, the framework enables reliable and adaptive operation under feedstock uncertainty, supporting resilient biogas-to-methanol production systems.

title: Techno-Economic Optimization of Seasonal Cold Thermal Energy Storage: Integrated Operation Scheduling and Storage Sizing under Time-of-Use Tariffs
affiliations: Jiangsu University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Techno-Economic Optimization of Seasonal Cold Thermal Energy Storage: Integrated Operation Scheduling and Storage Sizing under Time-of-Use Tariffs
detail.abstract: Seasonal cold thermal energy storage (SCTES) has emerged as a promising strategy for reducing cooling energy consumption, peak electricity demand, and associated carbon emissions by utilizing naturally available winter cold energy for summer cooling applications. However, the economic feasibility of SCTES remains uncertain because storage capacity, operational scheduling, and electricity tariff structures interact in complex ways that strongly influence lifecycle performance. This study develops a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP)-based techno-economic optimization framework that simultaneously determines storage sizing and hourly operation scheduling under Korean time-of-use tariffs, using building energy management system data from a Korean research campus and a 30-year lifecycle assessment period. Results show that SCTES can reduce peak chiller operation and electricity costs, with seasonal-only operation achieving the most favorable performance at approximately 20-30% storage capacity, while integrated seasonal and peak-shift operation exhibits lower LCOS at moderate storage levels but deteriorating economics with oversized storage. These findings indicate that tariff-sensitive operational scheduling and optimized storage sizing are more influential than storage capacity alone, providing a practical framework for designing cost-effective SCTES systems under realistic operating conditions.

title: Degradation-Aware Electric Vehicle Charging Optimisation Considering Calendar and Cycle Ageing Under Realistic Operating Conditions​
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Degradation-Aware Electric Vehicle Charging Optimisation Considering Calendar and Cycle Ageing Under Realistic Operating Conditions​
detail.abstract: Battery degradation is increasingly recognised as the dominant cost factor in electric vehicle (EV) charging, yet it is often neglected or simplified in existing optimisation strategies. This paper proposes a degradation-aware decentralised charging framework that jointly minimises electricity acquisition cost and battery ageing cost, explicitly accounting for both calendar and cycle degradation mechanisms under realistic operating conditions.A semi-empirical ageing model is implemented for NMC lithium-ion cells, capturing the influence of temperature, state of charge and cycling conditions. Degradation is monetised using real battery market data and incorporated into a nonlinear programming (NLP) optimisation solved independently at each charging point.Results based on real Iberian electricity market data show that battery degradation cost can exceed electricity cost by up to a factor of four, fundamentally altering optimal charging strategies. The proposed method achieves a total cost reduction of 33.78% compared to Plug & Charge and delivers seasonal savings of 40–60% over Plug & Charge and 6–25% over the best-performing conventional strategy (ALAP).The findings demonstrate that degradation-aware optimisation significantly modifies charging behaviour and is essential for cost-effective and lifetime-preserving EV operation in real-world scenarios.

title: A bi-level scheduling model of battery swapping station cluster operator considering user's multi-utility under spatiotemporal aggregation
affiliations: North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University, University of Science and Technology Beijing, North China Electric Power University and North China Electric Power University

detail.title: A bi-level scheduling model of battery swapping station cluster operator considering user's multi-utility under spatiotemporal aggregation
detail.abstract: The battery swapping station cluster operator is a critical distributed flexible resource in the new-type power system. Enhancing synergy between swapping stations and renewable energy (RE) through spatiotemporal aggregation and user response is crucial for improving system flexibility and RE consumption. To this end, this study proposes a bi-level scheduling model for a battery swapping station cluster operator considering users’ multi-utility under spatiotemporal aggregation. Firstly, a closed-loop optimization framework integrating spatiotemporal prediction, dynamic decision-making, and user response is constructed, incorporating user behavior clustering and a road network distance decay model to achieve fine-grained station-level demand forecasting. Secondly, a bi-level Stackelberg game scheduling model is established: the upper-level objectives maximize net-load-to-RE matching and operator profit, while the lower-level objective maximizes user satisfaction, with a dynamic pricing mechanism and robust optimization addressing uncertainties. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed model is verified through a case study. The results show that it reduces prediction errors by 32%, achieves an RE matching RMSE of 0.406, an average daily profit of 158,000 CNY, and user satisfaction of 85%, while demonstrating strong robustness under extreme scenarios. This research provides a systematic solution for battery swap station clusters to balance environmental performance, economic efficiency, and user experience during operator dispatch.

title: Short-Term Probabilistic Forecasting of Parking Occupancy Rates Using a Quantile TCN–LSTM Network
affiliations: Kunming University of Science and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Kunming University of Science and Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Short-Term Probabilistic Forecasting of Parking Occupancy Rates Using a Quantile TCN–LSTM Network
detail.abstract: Accurate parking occupancy forecasting plays a vital role in addressing parking shortages and relieving traffic congestion. The QR-TCN-LSTM framework proposed here integrates quantile regression into a hybrid TCN–LSTM architecture, enabling explicit uncertainty quantification alongside adaptive feature selection. Experiments spanning six parking facility types and two forecasting horizons (15 min and 60 min) cover point, interval, and probabilistic forecasting. At the 15-min horizon, the model achieves an MAE of 0.007163 and a MAPE of 1.3447%, with stable performance retained at 60 min. For interval forecasting, average CWC values of 0.4429 (15 min) and 1.3838 (60 min) are obtained, representing a maximum reduction of 59.01% over baseline models. The results demonstrate that quantile regression, when embedded in a TCN–LSTM architecture, yields prediction intervals that are both compact and well-calibrated, offering a reliable solution for parking occupancy forecasting.

title: The structure of infrastructure adoption: competition of hydrogen and electric for long-haul freight decarbonization
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology - The H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial & Systems Engineering (ISyE) and Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: The structure of infrastructure adoption: competition of hydrogen and electric for long-haul freight decarbonization
detail.abstract: Long-haul freight decarbonization requires deploying new energy infrastructure—hydrogen refueling stations (HRS), electric charging, or emerging alternatives—across networks designed around incumbent diesel supply. Existing planning tools answer where to place stations but typically treat node-level refueling demand as a uniform or exogenously specified input, ignoring how it emerges from the coupling between freight flows and technology adoption dynamics. This paper develops a network-coupled deployment framework that integrates Bass diffusion adoption with a reinforcement-learning agent sequencing HRS installation under capital constraints. Applied to an empirical long-haul freight network derived from U.S. Freight Analysis Framework data (southeastern U.S. corridors) over a 50-year horizon, with systematic variation of carbon pricing, hydrogen cost trajectory, and deployment pace, the framework yields three quantitative findings. First, deployment pace provides a non-linear benefit: in the studied SE-US network, the adoption midpoint follows an empirical reciprocal relation t₀(k) ≈ 14.3/k + 15 (R² = 0.999), so that installing two or more stations per year activates the network and drives widespread adoption within roughly two decades, while installing more than four per year provides little additional benefit. Second, network position drives order-of-magnitude differences in node-level refueling demand—a high-centrality hub such as Atlanta exceeds 6.5 × 10⁸ kg/year at saturation under accelerated deployment while peripheral hubs generate roughly ten times less—challenging uniform station sizing assumptions. Third, the long-run fuel-cell electric truck (FCET) versus battery electric truck (BET) market split reduces to a linear function of the network's range advantage, ≈ 0.22 + 0.74ρ (R² = 1.00), where ρ is the fraction of tonne-hour capacity on corridors exceeding the BET range; this saturation relation is largely insensitive to fuel-cost dynamics once hydrogen reaches diesel parity. Together, these findings show that the long-run competition between hydrogen and battery-electric trucks is structured by two underlying mechanisms—deployment-pace activation and network-position-driven demand heterogeneity—yielding transferable scaling relationships for capital-constrained infrastructure planning.

title: Optimization-based operation of a hydrogen refuelling station: lexicographic hybrid predictive control with multi-arrival readiness and opportunistic priority-level skipping
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Optimization-based operation of a hydrogen refuelling station: lexicographic hybrid predictive control with multi-arrival readiness and opportunistic priority-level skipping
detail.abstract: The operation of a Hydrogen Refuelling Station (HRS) imposes two structural challenges on optimization-based control. First, the operator pursues incommensurable competing objectives (refuelling availability, energy eﬃciency, economic benefit) ranked by a policy-imposed hierarchy; a weighted scalar cost requires extensive tuning to prevent economic objectives from dominating operational readiness or vice versa. Second, HRS dynamics combine continuous mass-and-pressure evolution with discrete, event-triggered behaviours governed by logic-based rules that purely continuous formulations cannot capture accurately. This paper proposes a Lexicographic Hybrid Model Predictive Control (L-HMPC) framework for an on-site renewable HRS serving Heavy-Duty Fuel-Cell V ehicles (HDFVs). The HRS is modelled using the Mixed Logical Dynamical formalism, which captures hydrogen flows, pressure dynamics, valve logic and event-triggered refuelling in a linear mixed-integer structure. An algebraic abstraction of a multi-arrival availability metric encodes the combinatorial dispensing logic. Two control layers are designed: a supervisory L-HMPC for non-refuelling mode with lexicographic priority ordering, and an event-triggered HMPC for refuelling mode. An Opportunistic Priority-Level Skipping (OPLS) procedure bypassing near-optimal priority levels mitigates the sequential pipeline’s computational burden. Validation in silico uses a real HRS with on-site electrolysis, photo- voltaic generation, battery storage and cascaded hydrogen storage, under scenario-based stochastic HDFV demand over five summer days. Across all configurations, nearly every refuelling event is fulfilled, lexicographic decisions remain interpretable, and net electricity exchange intensities of−25.9 to 0.1 kWh/kg indicate net export to the grid in most cases. OPLS reduces median per-call solving time by 39–49% and overall simulation time by 43%, without hindering operational or energy performance.

title: Possible Contribution of Smart EV Charging and PV Curtailment to Mitigating Low Voltage Grid Congestions – a Simulation Study
affiliations: Vinnytsia National Technical University, University for Continuing Education Krems and University for Continuing Education Krems

detail.title: Possible Contribution of Smart EV Charging and PV Curtailment to Mitigating Low Voltage Grid Congestions – a Simulation Study

keywords.keywords: Smart GridDemand ResponseCongestion MitigationLoad ManagementPV CurtailmentEV Charging

detail.abstract: The charging of electric vehicles (EV) causes a significant demand for renewable energy. The EV charging is nicely control-able and should maximally use varying renewable sources: (a) to be charged from renewable sources and (b) to support the balancing need. Power flows, and hence electricity production, are determined by the demand. The demand needs to be adjusted to the availability of power to optimally use varying power sources,. The work presented uses the physical impact of loads on the local supply voltage to control EV charging, flexible loads, and PV production. The supply voltage communicates changes in real time and links the distributed smart control mechanisms into a swarm of cooperative autonomous systems. The event based simulation applies stochastic modelling and effective power flow analysis. The graphical results show that the daily peaks caused by PV generation and EV charging can be mitigated to the benefit of the supply voltage, the PV generation, and the EV charging. Numeric results show that for the evaluated scenario, PV curtailment can be mostly prevented, such that the PV output is raised by ∼120 kWh, and that smart EV charging sufficiently covers the daily demand ≤ 24 kWh. In conclusion, smart EV charging benefits local PV production, stabilises the supply voltage, and serves EV drivers well, if a sufficient number of EVs is available for smart EV charging to consume the local PV peak effectively.

title: Long-Term Real-Life Evaluation of an Innovative Dew Point Evaporative Cooling for Edge Data Centre
affiliations: University of Hull, University of Hull, Kingston University, University of Hull, University of Hull and University of Hull

detail.title: Long-Term Real-Life Evaluation of an Innovative Dew Point Evaporative Cooling for Edge Data Centre
detail.abstract: Small-scale edge data centres and server rooms are expanding with digitalisation, AI deployment and distributed computing, but their cooling systems are often less efficient than those in large data centres. This paper presents, to the authors’ knowledge, the first full-year real-life monitoring study of an innovative dew-point evaporative cooling (DPC) system installed in a live edge data centre in the UK. The study moves DPC evaluation beyond laboratory testing and short-term prototype trials towards higher technology readiness under practical operating conditions. The system was assessed using performance mapping, full-year monitoring data, seasonal temperature profiles, hourly summer-event analysis and microbiological monitoring. During annual operation, the DPC system provided effective indoor temperature management, with monthly average COP values generally between 27 and 36 during normal operating periods. However, the COP reduced to approximately 18 during the constrained summer operation in July. The analysis shows that DPC performance depends not only on the heat and mass exchanger, but also on system-level factors such as installation arrangement, outdoor conditions, ductwork, airflow management and interaction with existing split units. Microbiological monitoring showed that no dip-slide sample exceeded the unacceptable threshold when a bespoke risk management protocol was applied. The results demonstrate that DPC can provide high-COP, low-electricity base cooling for small edge data centres. However, successful deployment requires appropriate system-level design, hybrid control with auxiliary split units, and low-burden water-side maintenance strategies. These findings provide first-hand long-term field evidence for the practical application of innovative DPC technology in edge data centre cooling.

title: Market-Informed Feature Engineering for Day-Ahead Price Forecasting in ERCOT
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Market-Informed Feature Engineering for Day-Ahead Price Forecasting in ERCOT
detail.abstract: The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) operates an energy-only wholesale electricitymarket characterized by high renewable penetration, limited inter-grid connectivity, and scarcity-driven real-time pricing. These structural features produce pronounced price-spike dynamics thatmake day-ahead price forecasting both more di!cult and more consequential for market participants.Existing electricity price forecasting research relies predominantly on standardized feature sets,typically lagged prices and load forecasts, that often fail to explicitly encode grid-stress and scarcityconditions that drive spikes, and spike forecasting accuracy remains a challenge. This study addressesboth gaps through the development of a day-ahead forecasting model for the ERCOT North Load Zonewhich combines a market-informed feature set that captures underlying price-formation mechanismsand forecasts price spikes via a regime-switching random forest ensemble method (MoE-RF). Allinput data is restricted to information available to market participants before the 10h00 gate closure— the submission deadline for day-ahead market bids. Predictive accuracy is evaluated on a full out-of-sample year, 2024, and the MoE-RF model significantly outperforms SARIMAX, LEAR, and naivebenchmark models. Furthermore, this study tests whether data published after gate closure enhancespredictive accuracy and finds no measurable gain. This indicates that the feature set developed in thisstudy captures the dynamics relevant to price formation, underscoring the value in applying domainknowledge to feature engineering. It further demonstrates that respecting the gate closure deadlinecan be adopted as an explicit design requirement without sacrificing predictive accuracy.

title: Potential of Optimal Multi-Objective Demand Side Management in Integrated District Heating and Cooling Networks
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Geneva and Swiss Federal Laboratories for Material Science and Technology (EMPA)

detail.title: Potential of Optimal Multi-Objective Demand Side Management in Integrated District Heating and Cooling Networks

keywords: Integrated district heating and cooling networks

detail.abstract: The optimal operation of integrated district heating and cooling (DHC) networks requires flexibility to lower costs, reduce emissions, and mitigate peak loads. While these systems are often subject to inflexible, rule-based control (RBC) thermal demands, demand-side management (DSM) can leverage the thermal inertia of buildings as a zero-capital-cost source of flexibility. To study the potential benefits achievable through DSM, this study first translates detailed white-box building simulations into low-complexity, calibrated grey-box resistance-capacitance (RC) models to accurately represent a real DHC network in Zürich, Switzerland. Then, using a multi-objective optimization framework, we compare standard RBC against DSM. Results demonstrate that optimally coordinating building thermal demands achieves substantial benefits, including a 6.2% reduction in operational costs, a 91.1% reduction in carbon emissions, and peak load shaving of 24.5% for heating and 53.8% for cooling. Optimizing for individual benefits, however, imposes severe penalties across other metrics. Multi-dimensional Pareto surfaces highlight this inherent conflict and visualize the system's optimal operation space. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses reveal that dynamic hourly tariffs and relaxed lower-bound indoor temperatures are critical to increase DSM cost-saving potential. Moreover, the results indicate that under DSM, the distributed storage in the thermal mass of the buildings connected to the studied network are equivalent to an 800–900 kWh centralized thermal energy storage (TES) unit, representing 15 times the currently installed capacity, offering the potential to offset physical infrastructure investments in modern integrated DHC systems.

title: Integrating Photovoltaic-Thermal Systems, Multi-Energy Storage and Demand Response for Cost-Effective Sustainable Manufacturing Systems
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago, University of Illinois Chicago and University of Illinois at Chicago

detail.title: Integrating Photovoltaic-Thermal Systems, Multi-Energy Storage and Demand Response for Cost-Effective Sustainable Manufacturing Systems
detail.abstract: The manufacturing sector is a major contributor to global energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, highlighting the need for effective strategies to integrate on-site renewable energy and reduce fossil fuel dependence in industrial systems. Among renewable energy technologies, Photovoltaic-Thermal (PVT) systems represent a promising solution by simultaneously generating electricity and thermal energy, making them particularly suitable for manufacturing environments characterized by significant multi-energy demands.As one of the few studies integrating PVT systems, multi-energy storage, and Demand Response (DR) strategies within a unified manufacturing-oriented framework, the proposed approach explicitly models the interactions between production scheduling, Heating Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) operation, and multi-energy flows, enabling coordinated decision-making between manufacturing processes and energy management. To support the coordinated design and operation of the proposed system, a robust bilevel Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model is formulated, where the bilevel structure captures the hierarchical relationship between planning and operational decisions, while robust optimization accounts for weather uncertainty affecting PVT generation and ensures reliable system performance under adverse operating conditions.A case study based on a lithium-ion battery manufacturing facility in Phoenix, Arizona, demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Compared with a baseline scenario without renewable integration and DR, the optimized configuration achieves a 24.35% reduction in total annualized costs and an 11.9% decrease in CO2 emissions. A post-event analysis further confirms that the system maintains stable economic performance under increasingly adverse weather conditions. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of jointly optimizing energy systems and production operations, demonstrating that integrating PVT systems with multi-energy storage and DR strategies can significantly improve economic and environmental performance in industrial settings.

title: Coordinated Battery Swapping Scheduling via Time-Window Translation and Inventory-Coupled Price Recoordination
affiliations: Guangxi University, Dalian University of Technology, Inner Mongolia University of Technology, Hunan University, Linyi University, Linyi University, Guangxi University, Guangxi University - School of Electrical Engineering, Great Bay University and Inner Mongolia University of Technology

detail.title: Coordinated Battery Swapping Scheduling via Time-Window Translation and Inventory-Coupled Price Recoordination

keywords.keywords: Battery swapping staionTime-Aggregated schedulingTime-Window translationMixed integer linear programmingNon-zero-sum game

detail.abstract: Coordinating battery swapping demand at a single battery swapping station is challenging because individual users make discrete time-slot choices, while station operation is constrained by battery inventory, charging completion, and time-varying pricing. This paper develops a coordinated scheduling framework with time-window translation and inventory-coupled price recoordination. Each electric vehicle user (EVU) selects one feasible swapping slot, and the associated charging requirement is allowed to vary with the selected slot. A price-driven fixed-point recoordination procedure is then used to iteratively align user-side slot choices with station-side inventory evolution and service-price updates, yielding a physically feasible and economically consistent schedule. On top of the physical coordination layer, a fairness-aware post-correction mechanism is introduced to alleviate excessive disparities in cost savings among valley, flat, and peak user groups. Case studies based on station operation data show that the proposed framework reduces system cost, smooths the aggregate load profile, and improves inventory adequacy. The fairness-aware correction changes total cost only marginally while improving the balance of group-level benefits. The method is positioned as a feasibility-oriented coordination framework rather than a strict equilibrium solution.

title: Sisal Fiber-Reinforced Cement Plates: Performance Evaluation for an Ecofriendly Building Product​
affiliations: Rio de Janeiro State University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro and Rio de Janeiro State University

detail.title: Sisal Fiber-Reinforced Cement Plates: Performance Evaluation for an Ecofriendly Building Product​
detail.abstract: The construction industry faces significant environmental challenges, such as high carbon dioxide emissions and consumption of non-renewable resources. Vegetable fibers, such as sisal, have emerged as sustainable reinforcements for cementitious materials, offering favorable mechanical properties. This study evaluated cementitious plates reinforced with 5% aligned long sisal fibers. The matrix had 50% of the cement content replaced by metakaolin and fly ash to mitigate fiber degradation caused by alkaline attack. Mechanical and physical tests were conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Brazilian standard NBR 15498. Tensile stress in bending results showed a mean of 22.31 ± 4.56 MPa for the room condition and 19.07 ± 2.68 MPa for saturated condition. The material presented an apparent density of 1.72g/cm³, a water absorption of 13.81%, and maintained its mechanical strength after accelerated aging. The plates exhibited good dimensional stability under moisture variation and met the standard requirements for water permeability. Thus, sisal fiber-reinforced cementitious plates represent a competitive and potentially more sustainable alternative for the construction sector compared to materials currently available on the Brazilian market.

title: Biodiversity Risk Exposure and Analysts’ Forecasts
affiliations: The University of Western Australia - UWA Business School, The University of Western Australia and The University of Western Australia - UWA Business School

detail.title: Biodiversity Risk Exposure and Analysts’ Forecasts
detail.abstract: We document that greater corporate biodiversity risk exposure is associated with significantly lower earnings forecast accuracy and higher forecast dispersion among financial analysts. These effects are more pronounced for firms with higher earnings volatility or more opaque disclosure environments. Further analyses show that analysts’ professional experience, industry specialization, and biodiversity related expertise mitigate these effects. In addition, stronger stakeholder awareness of biodiversity issues attenuates the influence of biodiversity risk on analysts’ forecast accuracy and dispersion. Our findings highlight analysts’ information processing and forecasting behavior as an important channel through which biodiversity risk affects capital markets.

title: More Than Cosmetics: Exploring the Hedging Capabilities and Safe-Haven Properties of Video Game Skins
affiliations: Peking University HSBC Business School

detail.title: More Than Cosmetics: Exploring the Hedging Capabilities and Safe-Haven Properties of Video Game Skins
detail.abstract: As video game skins attract increasing attention from players and investors, the exponential growth of these secondary markets warrants financial examination.This paper examines Counter-Strike 2 skins, one of the most prominent virtual assets on Steam, as an emerging alternative asset class, utilizing a quantile-integrated Threshold GARCH model to evaluate their hedging capabilities.Empirical results demonstrate that CS2 skins exhibit a structural decoupling from traditional equity markets and serve as a robust safe haven during market recessions, offering a more stable risk profile than traditional cryptocurrencies.This hedging efficacy remains robust even after controlling for systemic macroeconomic uncertainties and global sentiment shocks.Furthermore, while simulating a mixed portfolio reveals significantly enhanced risk-adjusted returns, the practical implementation of such strategies remains constrained by market frictions as well as regulatory uncertainties.

title: Discrimination of Sedentary and Athletic Profiles via FTIR-Based Digital Fingerprints combined with Supervised Machine Learning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidade de Coimbra, University of Lisbon, Universidade de Coimbra, Universidade de Aveiro, Universidade de Coimbra, Universidade de Coimbra, Universidade de Coimbra, Universidade de Coimbra and Universidade de Coimbra

detail.title: Discrimination of Sedentary and Athletic Profiles via FTIR-Based Digital Fingerprints combined with Supervised Machine Learning
detail.abstract: Introduction: Physical inactivity is a major global health concern, while regular exercise yields well-documented physiological and metabolic benefits. Despite advances in molecular profiling, rapid, integrative, and cost-effective tools for assessing long-term adaptations to exercise remain limited. This study evaluated the potential of Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, combined with machine learning (ML) algorithms, to discriminate between sedentary individuals and trained athletes (football players and ultramarathon runners) using multiple aqueous biofluids. Methods: A total of 132 participants (87 athletes and 45 sedentary individuals) were assessed. FTIR spectra were obtained from five biological matrices: serum, plasma, capillary blood, urine, and saliva. Data preprocessing included baseline correction, vector normalization, and spectral truncation. Dimensionality reduction and classification were conducted using Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) and a range of supervised learning models (Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Random Forest, XGBoost and Decision Trees), with synthetic oversampling (SMOTE) applied within each cross-validation fold to address class imbalance. Data partitioning was performed at the participant level to prevent information leakage from repeated measures. Model performance was evaluated using cross-validation, with F1-score, area under the curve (AUC), balanced accuracy, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) as primary metrics; bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals were estimated for each. Results: The best-performing models were obtained with capillary blood, serum, and plasma. A Decision Tree classifier applied to capillary blood spectra achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.917 (95% CI: 0.820–1.000), a weighted F1-score of 0.914, and an AUC of 0.937. An XGBoost classifier trained on serum spectra achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.765 (95% CI: 0.623–0.893) and an AUC of 0.877. In plasma, an MLP classifier trained across all three collection timepoints achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.757 (95% CI: 0.643–0.875) and an AUC of 0.909. Urine and saliva yielded substantially lower predictive accuracy (balanced accuracy below 0.60). Biochemical analysis of key spectral regions identified distinct differences in lipid- and protein-related functional groups between sedentary individuals and trained athletes, consistent with physiological adaptations to chronic exercise [1, 2]. Conclusion: This is the first study to apply FTIR spectroscopy across multiple biofluids to stratify individuals based on chronic exercise status. The findings demonstrate that FTIR spectroscopy, coupled with ML, offers a promising, label-free, and scalable approach for profiling physiological adaptations to exercise. These results support its further development for use in sports medicine, precision health monitoring, and personalized exercise prescription.

title: Transport Costs, Commuting Time, and Labour Market Outcomes: Evidence from an Informal Urban Transport System
affiliations: University of Johannesburg, Makerere University Business School, Makerere University Business School and Kampala Capital City Authority

detail.title: Transport Costs, Commuting Time, and Labour Market Outcomes: Evidence from an Informal Urban Transport System
detail.abstract: In cities dominated by informal and unregulated public transport, commuting costs act as a tax on labour income, limiting access to formal employment and shaping the spatial distribution of workers. Evidence on this mechanism remains limited for East African cities. This paper extends the Spatial Mismatch Hypothesis by formalising transport affordability as a threshold-based constraint within an effective-wage framework, introducing a discrete labour market sorting mechanism.,Using a stratified cross-sectional survey of 3,421 employed adults in the Greater Kampala Metropolitan Area (GKMA), Uganda, we estimate binary and multinomial logistic models with robust standard errors. Commute time is the strongest transport correlate of formal employment: each additional 10 minutes is associated with a 2.2 percentage-point reduction in formal employment probability (AME = -0.022, p < 0.001), with larger effects among lowest-income workers (-7.0 pp per 10 min). Approximately 16.3% of workers face a high affordability burden (>30% of income) and are 20 percentage points more likely to have refused a better-paying job due to commuting costs. Workplace location is strongly associated with commuting conditions: deteriorating conditions reduce the likelihood of working in more accessible inner areas while increasing the probability of employment in more distant peri-urban locations.,These findings are consistent with transport affordability acting as a binding constraint on labour market outcomes in informal-transit systems. Reducing commute time is likely to yield larger labour market gains than fare interventions alone, while targeted subsidies and spatial investment can improve efficiency and access.

title: The Unintended Consequences of Mandatory Reserve Price to Private Equity Placement
affiliations: , Beijing Jiaotong University, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE)

detail.title: The Unintended Consequences of Mandatory Reserve Price to Private Equity Placement
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether reserve prices impact the discount on private equity placements (PEPs). Using a sample of auction-based PEPs in China, we find that reserve price discounts are positively associated with bid (offer) price discounts. This inference holds after executing several robustness checks. As extra analyses reveal, the documented impact is ascribed to bidders anchoring on reserve prices. The positive association also depends on bidder identity and anchor-target compatibility. Our evidence ultimately shows that investor wealth benefits from such anchoring biases. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that reserve prices induce bidder undervaluation, thereby resulting in lower offer prices.

title: High-Efficiency Gas Extraction via Mechanical Cavity Creation in Downward Boreholes Drilled from Roof Roadways

detail.title: High-Efficiency Gas Extraction via Mechanical Cavity Creation in Downward Boreholes Drilled from Roof Roadways
detail.abstract: To address the problems of low coal fragmentation efficiency, poor cuttings discharge, and insufficient gas extraction in downward drilling within roof roadways, this study proposes a mechanical cavity-creation technology for pressure relief and permeability enhancement. Using water as the control medium, the technology regulates water pressure to automatically open and close the cutting blades, thereby damaging the coal structure and improving permeability.Taking the Wu9 and Wu10 coal seams in Mine No. 8 of Pingdingshan Coal Mining Company as the engineering background, theoretical analysis, numerical simulation, and field tests were conducted to examine pressure-relief effects, damage evolution, permeability distribution, and gas extraction performance. Field application was performed at the Wu9,10-21070 working face.The results show that mechanical cavity creation significantly improves pressure relief and coal deformation. The radial pressure-relief zone expanded from 1.3 m to 6.2 m, while the maximum plastic deformation zone increased from 0.3 m to 3.75 m. The permeability-enhanced zone, where permeability increased by one order of magnitude, expanded from 0.95 m to 6.0 m. In addition, the effective gas extraction radius within 30–180 days increased by 1.94–2.14 times, indicating that the technology can shorten extraction time, reduce drilling quantity, and lower engineering costs.Field results further demonstrate that gas concentration and pure gas production per 100 m in cavity-forming sections were consistently higher than those in conventional sections. With a 70% reduction in drilling quantity, the pre-drainage period was shortened from 90 to 70 days. Roadway excavation speed increased from 4.2 m/d to 4.6 m/d, and maximum drill cuttings decreased from 4.5 kg/m to 3.9 kg/m. These findings confirm the effectiveness and applicability of the proposed technology for coal mine gas control.

title: Does Industrial Policy Persistence Produce Persistent Outcomes? An SPMC Framework Analysis of Policy Adoption and Economic Performance
affiliations: University of Dubrovnik

detail.title: Does Industrial Policy Persistence Produce Persistent Outcomes? An SPMC Framework Analysis of Policy Adoption and Economic Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could have influenced this study.

detail.abstract:
This paper applies the Sequential Probability Markov Chain (SPMC) framework, originally
developed for financial market regime detection, to the domain of industrial policy evaluation.
Using the Juhász, Lane, Ossa, and Pezerd (JLOP 2025) dataset of 47,283 policy measures across 15
countries (2000–2022), World Bank macroeconomic indicators, and UN Comtrade bilateral trade
flows, the analysis tests whether the documented persistence of industrial policy instrument
adoption translates into persistent economic outcomes.
The central finding is a stark asymmetry. Industrial policy instruments exhibit strong sequential
persistence (10 of 15 countries show statistically significant SPMC regime structure in their
adoption sequences, with grand autocorrelation AC1 = 0.42). Economic outcomes, by contrast,
show no persistence whatsoever. Manufacturing value-added growth exhibits zero significant
SPMC structure across all 15 countries. Export growth at both HS2 sector and HS6 product levels
is anti-persistent (grand AC1 = -0.065 for HS6 product growth, p = 0.001), meaning good years
actively predict bad years and vice versa.
Robustness tests reinforce the null. Difference-in-differences estimation comparing targeted and
non-targeted sectors finds no persistence differential (DiD = 0.042, 95% CI [-0.108, 0.188]).
Granger causality tests confirm that industrial policy instrument counts do not predict subsequent
GDP growth (p = 0.186). Chow structural break tests identify level shifts during the 2008–2009
crisis but no change in autocorrelation structure. Monte Carlo power analysis demonstrates that
detecting AC1 = 0.10 would require over 500 annual observations, placing the effect size below
what 22-year panels can reliably detect.
These results carry a direct implication for the mission-oriented industrial policy literature. Policy
adoption is path-dependent but outcomes are not. The stickiness of instrument choice reflects
bureaucratic and political momentum rather than cumulative economic impact. Evaluating
industrial policy through the lens of regime persistence reveals that the connection between doing
more of the same and getting more of the same is not supported by the data.

title: Experience, Memory, and the Timing of Disaster Preparation

detail.title: Experience, Memory, and the Timing of Disaster Preparation
detail.abstract: Natural disasters have become more frequent and severe causing some people to experience them multiple times in quick succession. Additionally, changes in weather patterns and atmospheric conditions have made previously predictable aspects of natural disasters less so. While increasing experience with disasters be give people opportunities to learn how to prepare, any long lapses between subsequent disasters be result in discounting of the disaster's severity. I study the effects of experience and discounting on the average response to natural disasters by analyzing sales of emergency supplies, namely bottle water, during the 2008-2019 Atlantic hurricane seasons. Through event study analysis, I find that increases in historical exposure have little effect on the responsiveness of consumers; however, consumers respond increasingly to current hurricanes as the length of time since the most recent hurricane increases.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a formal valuation and accounting framework for physical climate risk in commercial real estate (CRE), retail, logistics, and infrastructure-linked assets when conventional insurance ceases to operate as a reliable risktransfer mechanism. It bridges climate-risk disclosure and financial-statement measurement by introducing the Uninsurability Discount Factor (λ_climate), an annualized risk premium or expected-loss bridge that converts extreme-event probability, enforceable insurance-coverage deficits, and severity/liquidity frictions into auditable valuation inputs. The framework is anchored in IFRS 13 market-participant assumptions, IAS 36 impairment indicators and recoverable-amount testing, and IFRS S2 connectivity between climate-related risks, cash flows, access to finance, and cost of capital.
The paper strengthens the original framework by decomposing valuation variables into their economic intuition and accounting functions. Key contributions include:
Calibration of the Severity and Friction Coefficient (φ): Introducing a standardized weighting matrix incorporating lost rent, reconstruction burden, and liquidity friction, while requiring asset-level evidence and sensitivity analysis for Level 3 inputs.
 The Geographic Stigma Effect: Analyzing how the retreat of underwriters creates a systemic liquidity discount, even for assets with active policies, by impairing exit values and financing capacity. 
 Case-Based Valuation Simulations: Utilizing the 2023 California insurance crisis and the 2024 Rio Grande do Sul floods to demonstrate that conventional models can overstate Net Asset Value (NAV) by 21% to 30%. 
The methodology provides auditors, CFOs, valuation committees, and independent appraisers with a data-driven toolkit to connect sustainability disclosures with financial-statement measurement. By requiring explicit assessment of uninsurability before a disaster occurs - rather than automatic impairment - the framework improves capital allocation, strengthens audit documentation, and reduces the probability of abrupt climate-related write-offs when a known risktransfer failure has already become observable.

title: Towards a Concept of Ecological Sovereignty

detail.title: Towards a Concept of Ecological Sovereignty

contentType.other: Working Paper Series at a Research Institute

detail.abstract: Sovereignty is mostly articulated through a paradigm of interstate competition over resources and borders, in order to facilitate accumulation and control. Although its current appeal dates back to the seventeenth century and the Westphalian system, the definitions thus far privileged by the socalled international order have mostly worked against the interests of peoples and territories subject to (neo)colonial power, imperialism, and resource grabs. This working paper interrogates how the ideology of 'national interest' is mobilised by states to advance expansionist interests in ways that disregard planetary boundaries and solidaristic cooperation among peoples, ultimately to the detriment of demands for self-determination, and to the possibility of building the ecosocial just transitions necessary for overcoming the polycrisis. In counterpoint, the paper it suggests the need for a framework of popular and ecological sovereignty aimed at securing mutual survival and longevity. This , which will means learning from movements and political organisations that challenge the capital-nation-state fantasy of limitless growth, in order to reformulate the basis for production and consumption in accordance with radical sustainability and a good life for the world's majority. Alameda

title: Who Gets What: The Selectorate, the Winning Coalition, and the Distribution of Federal Benefits

detail.title: Who Gets What: The Selectorate, the Winning Coalition, and the Distribution of Federal Benefits

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no institutional affiliations.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The author used publicly available information. No participants were involved.

detail.abstract: The question 'does government help people?' is routinely asked wrong-as though government allocates resources neutrally rather than as an instrument of the winning coalition. This paper applies selectorate theory, Hohfeldian jural analysis, and cultural materialist political economy to the full $4.25 trillion FY2024 federal budget, allocating benefits to the eight coalitions identified in Paper P7 and deriving three formal metrics: the State Dependence Index (Dc), measuring total government support per capita; the Visibility Gap Index (Gc), measuring the proportion of that support arriving through invisible channels; and the Club-to-Broad Goods Ratio (C/B), measuring the concentration of selective versus universal benefits. The findings invert virtually every assumption embedded in American political discourse. The Elite coalition (4% of the population) receives $25,557 per capita in federal support-the highest of any coalition-with 88% arriving invisibly through tax expenditures, financial regulatory architecture, and macro-financial backstops. The Disaffected coalition (17.5%), stigmatized as the welfare-dependent population, receives $16,948 per capita-$8,609 less than Elite-with 96% arriving visibly through programs that generate political vulnerability. Finance and insurance sector workers receive $43,850 per worker annually in federal support, with 68% invisible; retail and service workers receive $11,200 with 85% visible. The analysis demonstrates that the American welfare state is not one system but two-an invisible welfare state serving the winning coalition through immunities and privileges, and a visible welfare state serving the losing coalition through claim-rights-and that the political conflict over 'government spending' is a conflict between these two systems in which one side's benefits are defined as welfare and the other's are defined as earned income. A tenscenario sensitivity analysis confirms that the structural pattern-Elite per capita exceeds Disaffected per capita; the visibility inversion persists-survives all reasonable parameter variations.

title: New Technologies and the Labor Share. A Share-Altering Representation
affiliations: University of Siena - Department of Economics and Statistics and University of Siena - Department of Economics

detail.title: New Technologies and the Labor Share. A Share-Altering Representation
detail.abstract: We propose a share-altering framework with constant-returns-to-scale Cobb-Douglas production functions which accommodates for several forms of technical progress (capital-skill complementarity, robotization, AI-type technological change). The model is consistent with stylized facts, such as increasing wage inequality driven by skill-biased technical change or robotization, and provides insights into the potentially nuanced consequences of AI adoption on the wage distribution. We also extend the model to consider the production of new inputs. We show that the introduction of new inputs, despite their positive impact on the labor demand, will reduce the labor share whenever they replace tasks previously performed by workers.

title: Internal Mobility Barriers and Firm Productivity: Evidence from a Spatial Discontinuity in China
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) and

detail.title: Internal Mobility Barriers and Firm Productivity: Evidence from a Spatial Discontinuity in China
detail.abstract: How do barriers to mobility within cities shape firm performance and urban welfare? This paper studies Shenzhen’s Second Line, a historical internal boundary that restricts labor mobility within the city until its relaxation in 2003. Using firm-level data from China’s Annual Survey of Industrial Firms and the historical geography of the boundary, we implement a boundary-based difference-in-discontinuities design that compares firms located just inside and just outside the Second Line before and after the reform. We find that firms inside the boundary experience productivity gains of approximately 20 percent following the relaxation, with similar estimates across OP, LP, and ACF productivity measures. The results are robust to alternative bandwidths, donut regression discontinuity specifications, difference-in-differences estimators, and alternative fixed-effect. We then develop a quantitative spatial model to quantify the welfare effects of relaxing the Second Line, decompose these effects into productivity and amenity channels, and conduct counterfactual analyses that underscore the importance of reduced migration frictions in shaping the observed productivity gains.

title: Image Concerns in Organizations

detail.abstract:
This paper provides a formal analysis of social image concerns and their motivational effects within teams and organizations. Agents are characterized by private attributes capturing individual self-interest, prosocial concern for the organization, and social image concerns. Assuming that agents value being perceived as organizationally concerned, we derive the principal's optimal incentive contract and characterize the resulting effort levels under various conditions. Image concerns give rise to reputational incentives; however, these are attenuated by monetary incentives, leading to lower-powered optimal contracts. Nevertheless, image concerns benefit organizations by mitigating the free-rider problem and giving rise to positive peer effects in the workplace. The paper provides a novel microfoundation for positive team effects based on endogenous reputational incentives and offers a resolution to the team-size puzzle. We extend the model to incorporate image concerns related to self-interest as well as hierarchical image concerns vis-à-vis a manager.
Finally, we present a range of organizational applications, illustrating how team size, team diversity, and the presence of outsiders can enhance image concerns, work incentives, and overall firm performance. We discuss implications for teams, organizations, and corporate culture.

title: Coal Dependence, Structural Persistence, and Population Health in Southeast Asia
affiliations: University of Edinburgh - Edinburgh Business School, University of Edinburgh Business School, Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics and University of London

detail.title: Coal Dependence, Structural Persistence, and Population Health in Southeast Asia
detail.abstract: Energy transitions affect welfare not only through aggregate energy use or carbon emissions, but also through the structural position of specific fuels within national energy systems. This paper examines whether coal dependence remains central to the energy-health relationship in Southeast Asia, whether renewable energy expansion has begun to displace that centrality, and whether the observed pattern is regionally specific. Using an unbalanced panel of all ten ASEAN economies over 1990-2020, we adapt a rolling weighted-degree diagnostic, termed Aggregated Influence Scores (AIS), that tracks persistent systemic centrality within the energy-health correlation network, and combine it with two-way fixed-effects panel regression. Permutation-validated AIS results show that coal has the highest mean structural centrality in the regional energy-health network and retains this position throughout the sample despite rising renewable integration. Renewable energy exhibits structural emergence from the mid-2000s but does not displace coal or generate a stable life-expectancy association. Panel regressions provide qualified supporting evidence: coal consumption is negatively associated with life expectancy in the core ASEAN panel (β =-7.34, p < 0.001; Driscoll-Kraay inference), with the sign remaining negative across more than twenty specifications. The association captures medium-term within-country co-movement and should not be interpreted as a causal effect, long-run equilibrium parameter, or exposure-response coefficient. Extended-panel benchmarking across 38 developing economies yields a more conservative Southeast Asian estimate (β =-1.02, p = 0.042), which is treated as the preferred benchmark for policy appraisal; the association is not significant outside Southeast Asia. The findings support evaluating coal phasedown for potential regional health co-benefits and show that renewable capacity addition without coal displacement may represent structural transition without welfare translation.

title: Over-indebtedness and Tenure Status
affiliations: University of Granada and University of Granada

detail.title: Over-indebtedness and Tenure Status
detail.abstract: Using the panel structure of the Spanish Household Finances Survey (SHF) from 2002 to 2022, this paper examines how housing tenure shapes household financial fragility in Spain by adapting standard indicators of over-indebtedness to treat rental payments analogously to mortgage repayments and to incorporate the full range of household debt obligations. The analysis argues that conventional measures of financial fragility systematically underestimate the vulnerability of tenants by excluding rental obligations. We also explore heterogeneity by household composition, marital status, age, and macroeconomic conditions. The results reveal a strong tenure gradient in financial vulnerability. Tenants are significantly more exposed to financial stress than outright homeowners, while mortgaged homeowners occupy an intermediate position. Standard indicators underestimate tenants' vulnerability, whereas augmented measures that incorporate rental payments increase their probability of overindebtedness by up to 24 percentage points. Financial fragility is particularly pronounced among single-earner, single, and younger households, and tenure gaps widen during economic downturns, especially following the COVID-19 shock. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of incorporating rental housing costs to accurately assess household financial vulnerability.

title: Cloud Capital's Hidden Thirst: Technofeudalism, Scope 2 Water Concealment, and AI Infrastructure Externalities

detail.title: Cloud Capital's Hidden Thirst: Technofeudalism, Scope 2 Water Concealment, and AI Infrastructure Externalities
detail.abstract: This paper examines the environmental externalities of artificial intelligence infrastructure through the theoretical lens of Yanis Varoufakis' concept of Technofeudalism. Drawing on data from the 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory U.S. Data Center Energy Usage Report, peerreviewed water footprint research, and corporate sustainability disclosures, we argue that Big Tech's selective efficiency reporting-specifically its near-universal omission of Scope 2 (indirect) water consumption from sustainability reports-constitutes a structural externalization of cost consistent with Technofeudal accumulation logic. We show that Scope 2 water consumption is CLOUD CAPITAL'S HIDDEN THIRST estimated at 4-12 times greater than reported Scope 1 figures, and that the industry's reliance on Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) as a reporting standard actively incentivizes higher water consumption through evaporative cooling substitution. We examine the tension between PUE and Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) as an efficiency paradox with no current technical resolution, and survey regulatory solutions. We conclude that cloud capital accumulates precisely by externalizing its material costs onto local ecologies-and that meaningful accountability requires mandatory Scope 2 water disclosure standards.

detail.abstract:
This policy intelligence report examines the accelerating transformation of the global digital asset regulatory landscape and evaluates the strategic implications for Ghana, the ECOWAS region, and broader African financial governance. Issued by the Chamber of Digital Assets and Blockchain Innovations as the third volume in the West African Harmony series, the report synthesizes major international developments between January and April 2026, including the United States SEC-CFTC joint crypto asset classification framework, Kenya’s implementation of its Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASP) regime, Singapore’s institutional digital asset model, Ethiopia’s transition toward regulated oversight, and the growing systemic role of stablecoins in global payments infrastructure.

The report situates Ghana’s Virtual Asset Service Providers Act, 2025 (Act 1154) within a rapidly evolving international regulatory environment characterized by heightened anti-money laundering obligations, expanding stablecoin adoption, rising illicit on-chain activity, and intensified competition among jurisdictions seeking to attract compliant digital asset innovation. Drawing on regulatory analysis, comparative policy evaluation, FATF guidance, and regional market data, the study identifies both the opportunities and vulnerabilities facing Ghana and the ECOWAS region as digital assets become increasingly integrated into cross-border payments, remittances, institutional finance, and financial inclusion systems.

Particular attention is devoted to the implementation challenges of Ghana’s emerging framework, including token classification, Travel Rule compliance, VASP licensing architecture, taxation design, sanctions screening, and inter-agency coordination between financial regulators. The report further advances the West Africa Digital Asset Regulatory Readiness Initiative (WADARRI) as a proposed regional harmonization mechanism intended to strengthen supervisory capacity, reduce regulatory fragmentation, and align ECOWAS jurisdictions with evolving global standards.

In addition to regulatory analysis, the report explores the strategic implications of cedi-backed stablecoins, central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), blockchain-enabled remittance infrastructure, and the growing convergence between traditional financial institutions and digital asset markets. The study concludes that Ghana occupies a uniquely advantageous position as an early regulatory mover within West Africa, but that the effectiveness of this position depends on the timely completion of implementing instruments, proportional compliance structures, and sustained regional cooperation.

This report contributes to ongoing policy discourse on digital asset governance, financial innovation, and regional economic integration in Africa, while providing institutional recommendations for regulators, policymakers, financial intelligence authorities, tax agencies, and virtual asset service providers operating within emerging markets.

title: Adapting to Energy Scarcity: Evidence on Technological Change from UK Industry
affiliations: Cardiff University - Cardiff Business School, University of Southampton - Faculty of Economic, Social and Political Sciences and World Bank

detail.title: Adapting to Energy Scarcity: Evidence on Technological Change from UK Industry
detail.abstract: Climate change, geopolitical conflicts, and the AI thirst for power suggests that technological innovation that changes the production process by saving on the energy input will become a key factor in the coming future to ensure stable economic growth and low inflation. We analyse the UK industrial sector in the last 50 years to quantitatively assess the importance of energy innovation, characterise its evolution over time, and to understand how much of it is induced innovation. As innovation is a long-term process, we develop a new procedure that builds on an econometric approach that is well-suited to extract the low-frequency component of energy demand and energy price. We find that energy-saving technological change has allowed to save for energy at a rate of 2.3% each year in the last fifty years, with the consequence that today's energy consumption is one third of what it would have been in the absence of innovation. Moreover, we estimate that 38% of this innovation is induced by the long-run path of energy prices.

detail.title: Goals of the AfCFTA Competition Protocol Digital Market Competition Regulations: Lessons from South Africa’s Online Intermediation Platform Market Inquiry (OIPMI), The EU DMA and the us Experiences with Digital Platform Giants
detail.abstract:
The European Union (EU) has continued to be a worldwide leader in setting international norms, particularly in competition law policy, data protection and platform governance. In digital market regulation, after the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA), several countries have adopted or are considering the adoption of digital markets competition regulations (DMCR) similar to the DMA. While some have challenged the notion that the DMA and its goals of ensuring contestability and fairness in the market should not be the blueprint for adopting DMCRs in other countries, at this juncture, it is impossible to overstate the influence of the EU DMA on future DMCRs. We contribute towards this scholarly debate on the influence of the DMA beyond the EU by focusing on a region that, despite competition agencies' regulatory enforcement in digital markets, has not received adequate scholarly attention: Africa. Although no African country has considered adopting a DMCR at the continental level, African countries seek to adopt a DMCR under the AfCFTA Competition Protocol (CP). 

In formulating the appropriate goals of the AfCFTA DMCR, we build on African experiences in enforcing competition law, the African market structure, the debate on the goals of competition law in Africa, intellectual thinking on regulation of digital markets and the EU DMA. More specifically, for the Afri- can context, we draw on the 2023 Competition Commission of South Africa, Online Intermediation Platforms Market Inquiry (OIPMI) findings on business user treatment to further inform the appropriate goals of the AfCFTA DMCR. An analysis of the OIPMI Final Report shows that African markets have high
barriers to entry, and digital platforms impose unfair trading conditions on African businesses compared to international businesses. Consequently, like the EU DMA, fairness and contestability are critical for the success of African businesses in the digital markets. Given that public interest considerations will continue to shape African competition law enforcement in digital markets, African countries can draw from the insights of the EU Ordoliberal thinking as related
to the currently dissipated US New Brandeisian movement, both of which seek to enhance the participation of small businesses in a market characterized by few firms with concentrated economic power. We conclude by recommending
that, unlike the DMA, in which the goals are distinct from competition law, the AfCFTA DMCR should incorporate multiple goals merging regulatory goals with those of competition law enforcement, while prioritizing innovation, inclusivity, fairness, and contestability.

title: Online Demand for Credence Foods: Evidence from Organic and Non-GMO Beverages on Amazon
affiliations: Kentucky State University

detail.title: Online Demand for Credence Foods: Evidence from Organic and Non-GMO Beverages on Amazon
detail.abstract: Although a large literature examines consumer demand for credence foods in traditional retail settings, much less is known about how such demand extends to digital marketplaces. This paper investigates how organic and Non-GMO certification labels shape consumer demand in online food retail markets. Using high-frequency, product-level data from the tea and coffee categories on Amazon in the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (US), I estimate the influence of verified certification labels on product demand and the responsiveness of demand to price changes across heterogeneous products. The results show that organic and Non-GMO beverages command a significant sales premium, averaging approximately 12 percent. This premium varies across the sales distribution, ranging from about 8 percent at the 25th sales quantile to roughly 25 percent at the 75th quantile. Demand for certified beverages is also substantially less price-elastic, suggesting stronger consumer loyalty and greater pricing power for certified products in digital markets. The estimated demand patterns vary systematically across countries (UK vs. US), product types (tea vs. coffee), and seller types (Amazon vs. third-party sellers). Overall, the findings provide new evidence on how credence labels drive product differentiation and pricing strategies in rapidly expanding online food retail markets.

title: Deep Learning for Solving and Estimating Dynamic Models in Economics and Finance
affiliations: University of Lausanne - School of Economics and Business Administration (HEC-Lausanne)

detail.title: Deep Learning for Solving and Estimating Dynamic Models in Economics and Finance
detail.abstract:
This script offers an implementation-oriented introduction to deep learning methods for solving and estimating high-dimensional dynamic stochastic models in economics and finance.  Its starting point is the curse of dimensionality: heterogeneous-agent economies, overlapping-generations models with aggregate risk, continuous-time models with occasionally binding constraints, climate-economy models, and macro-finance environments with many assets and frictions all generate state and parameter spaces that strain classical tensor-product grid methods.

The exposition is organized around four complementary methodologies.  Deep Equilibrium Nets embed discrete-time equilibrium conditions directly into neural-network loss functions.  Physics-Informed Neural Networks approximate continuous-time Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman, Kolmogorov forward, and related partial differential equations.  Deep surrogate models provide fast, differentiable approximations to expensive structural models, while Gaussian processes add a probabilistic layer that quantifies approximation uncertainty; together they support estimation, sensitivity analysis, and constrained policy design.  Gaussian-process-based dynamic programming, combined with active learning and dimension reduction, extends value-function iteration to settings with very large continuous state spaces.

Applications range from representative-agent and international real business cycle models to overlapping-generations and heterogeneous-agent economies, continuous-time macro-finance, structural estimation by simulated method of moments, and climate economics under uncertainty.  The emphasis throughout is practical: economic restrictions are translated into trainable residuals, algorithms are paired with diagnostics, and companion notebooks in TensorFlow and PyTorch invite students to experiment, modify, and learn by doing.

These notes are not intended as an exhaustive textbook.  They are a deliberately subjective and inevitably incomplete snapshot of a rapidly evolving field.  The selection of architectures, references, and case studies reflects one researcher's judgment about useful entry points at the time of writing.  Their purpose is to equip PhD students and researchers with enough conceptual and computational machinery to engage with this frontier hands-on.

title: Threshold Heterogeneity in Green Bond Eects on Corporate Green Innovation: Causal Machine Learning Evidence from Green Knowledge Accumulation

detail.abstract: Do green bonds promote green innovation for all rms? Using 43,963 rm-year observations of A-share listed rms (20122023), this paper employs a three-layer identication design combining Double/Debiased Machine Learning (DML) with panel xed eects DID to examine threshold heterogeneity in green bond eects on corporate green innovation. The full-sample DML average treatment eect is insignicant (invention patent ATE =-0.004, p = 0.94). DML-residual heterogeneity screening identies pre-issuance green patent base (PreGreen) as the only variable surviving multiple testing correction among six candidates. Subgroup analysis reveals a binary threshold eect: rms with zero PreGreen exhibit a signicant decline in green invention patents (ATE =-0.202, p = 0.0007), consistent with compliance crowding-out; rms with positive PreGreen show a signicant increase (ATE = +0.361, p = 0.0007), consistent with innovation promotion. These ndings are local to the common support region and do not generalize to a universal pattern. The green knowledge accumulation threshold hypothesis advances the Porter hypothesis from whether it holds to when it holds.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a methodological framework for sequential conditioning of momentum-based signals on implied volatility regimes and distributional asymmetry in the S&P 500. Volatility is proxied through VIX regime dynamics relative to adaptive trend behaviour, momentum through exponential movingaverage structures, and asymmetry through rolling skewness of returns.
